title: The Clock Tower Mystery
markdown:
Catrin remembered Oakhaven as a town where time sang. Every clock, from the grand square tower to the baker’s little chime, kept the same beat, as if the hours had agreed in writing. Then one morning, at noon, sixty seconds went missing. A tiny gap in the town’s hum, like a skipped stair.

She was the clock apprentice. She knew every tick and groan in the tower the way other people know a house at night. Looking up the ladder still flipped her stomach. The rungs felt icy. Ash, her jackdaw, nudged her with a beak that had no patience for poetry.

“Fix it, Catrin. Something’s wrong.”

The Mayor’s speech was at one o’clock sharp. If the clocks lied, he would fluster and the square would argue with itself. This was more than a glitch. “Ash,” she whispered, “we have to find out why.” She took a breath that tasted of oil and old dust, and put her hands on the cold iron. A real tick-tock problem, not a textbook one.

They were still on the stairs when the Mayor began to boom. He was early. Tie askew, hair as if the wind had voted. The grand clock stood two minutes behind. People grumbled in the polite way of a town that likes its minutes numbered. Catrin’s heart sank a floor.

She and Ash raced the rooftops, tiles ticking under her boots. Ash spotted a dusty trail toward the old Clockmaker’s Guildhall. She followed, legs shaky, stubbornness growing a spine. The Guildhall was usually a comfort: gears, oil, the smell of work. Today silence hung in it like a coat on the wrong peg. On the highest turret, a dizzying perch, she opened her notebook. The diagrams were supposed to be the answer. A fierce gust arrived without asking and snatched the pages. They scattered like a second flock. The vital sheet, the master lever’s plan, fluttered over the edge.

“Oh, no.”

“Don’t worry.” Ash circled. He pointed at a rickety ledge. “Sometimes you have to get your beak dirty.”

The ledge was a suggestion of stone. The paper had snagged on a gargoyle’s ear, a stone grin that had seen better centuries. Her hands slicked. Her stomach performed its old trick. She pictured the confused Mayor, the impatient square, the silent gears. Oakhaven needed the minute back more than she needed a sensible distance from heights. She breathed, and made the paper the only object in the world. Inch by inch she stretched. Fingertips brushed grit, then pulp. She snatched it. Her body buzzed, not with the old wobble exactly, but with a bright, sharp thrill. She had the plan. She had not fallen.

They raced inside. The Regulator Chamber door was sealed: no keyhole, no handle, only brass that refused. Ash pecked it, offended. On the crumpled diagram Catrin found a tiny hidden symbol.

“The ventilation shaft.”

A dark narrow mouth, barely a squeeze. The speech below was running out of sentences. She peered in. Dust. Old time. Cobwebs like ghostly fingers. A whisper in her that said she could not. She pushed it down and slid after Ash, whose sharp calls became a beacon.

“This way. The rhythm is getting stronger.”

Cool metal. A faint whir. Her hand found a hidden lever. She pulled. A clunk travelled through the stone. The door swung.

The Central Regulator filled the chamber, magnificent and pulsing. Oil and metal clang. Her hands, at last, were steady. She adjusted a dial, tightened a spring that had been pretending to be tighter than it was. A soft hum returned, the right one. Outside, every town clock found its neighbour. One o’clock. Exactly. The Mayor blinked as if someone had handed him his place in the sentence. The square cheered, late and on time at once.

Catrin came out dusty. She climbed to the turret again. The wind whipped; she did not flinch. Oakhaven lay under a synchronized ticking, a choir that had remembered the words. Ash preened on her shoulder with a look that meant he had known. She stood in the weather and listened. The missing minute had gone back to work. She left the courage unnamed, and let the clocks do the talking.
